memories.memory_text: I remember getting fired up about Maestro’s crap fleet—calling them shit boxes felt good, and Darian Prescott didn’t back off, he leaned in, like he actually wanted to hear me rant.

He made that 'don’t seem like a girl who needs directions' comment—sounded like a line, but I played along, and when he said 'I’m Darian Prescott,' after that weird pause, I knew something had shifted.

I remember teasing Darian Prescott about his Concierge Key, holding my hands apart like I was guessing the size of his status number, saying 'I bet it's huge'—it came out way more suggestive than I meant, but I didn’t pull back.

After he said he hadn't hit his number yet, I just looked at him—really looked—and I remember the weight of the silence, how I didn’t look away, like I was letting something happen that I’d usually shut down.

I remember lying there after, both of us wrecked, and making a dumb joke about the towel rack—Darian Prescott actually laughed, and I said I liked how he’d wrapped me up in those stupid couch cushions like a human burrito.

We were both on our laptops, tossing out cities and dates—Albuquerque, Ft. Lauderdale—then just… typed each other in. No big talk, no promises. Just calendars syncing, like scheduling a meeting, but it felt like something more.

I told Darian Prescott not to worry about what's appropriate—there’s no room for that fake politeness between us, and if he wants to call, he should just do it. When he asked if I could push my layover, I smiled and said I could, and it felt like a small, real victory.
I texted Darian Prescott because I couldn't sleep, and he said he was awake too, just lying there—simple, but it felt like something shifted.

I walked into another hotel room with Darian Prescott, suitcases in hand, and didn’t even think twice about tossing my bag on the left bed—the one by the window. We didn’t say anything, but it just felt like we already knew the routine.

I saw her crying in the middle of the Eastgate Street, red-eyed and messy, and I just looked at her—probably like she’d lost her mind—before Darian Prescott introduced us like this was some kind of normal meet-cute.
I told Sawyer Adler that life can underwhelm you that way, and for a second, it felt like she actually heard me—not just the words, but the weight behind them.
I told Darian Prescott I googled him, and that it was what modern girls do when they have a crush—he looked surprised, maybe even caught off guard, and I remember feeling exposed saying it out loud.

We kissed after he told me about almost drowning and seeing the world from the helicopter—this one felt different, like we weren't just playing roles anymore, and then the boat died and we started laughing like idiots.

I remember Darian Prescott holding my wrist, saying he hadn’t enjoyed someone’s company like mine in a long time—and for once, I didn’t joke my way out of it. I just said, 'Neither can I,' and meant it.

I remember standing there in the parking lot, holding that stupid engagement the black photograph, and feeling my chest tighten when he asked me to the The Anniversary Game. I said no twice—'I can't,' 'I couldn't'—like my body knew before my mouth did how much this would change things.
After I finally said yes, he said we should kiss like it was some casual thing, but then I told him to just do it—'Then kiss me'—and when we did, it didn't feel like a joke anymore.
Darian Prescott and I walked through the terminal side by side, rolling our bags, and for no real reason we both cracked a smile—like we’d pulled off some quiet heist just by showing up together.
Harper Sawyer’s eyes locked onto me the second she opened that door, and the way she said ‘Darian Prescott has told me nothing about you’ made me feel like I’d been caught sneaking around.
When she asked if we were dating and I said ‘It’s not exactly…’, I could feel the weight of those words hanging there—like I’d just admitted we didn’t mean enough to name.
Darian Prescott tossed out an 'I love you' like it was a joke, but I could tell he wasn't entirely kidding—and I felt it, that weird weight in the room, like we both knew it wasn't just banter.

I stepped back in to grab that second box of flowers—Finley Hale was hauling them out for the The Anniversary Game setup—and said I’ve got it, just to give them space. I didn’t look back, but I knew the second I walked away, it was the first time in years the three of them were alone together.
I slid my hotel card into the window latch and popped it open—felt good to have something useful for once. Then I told Darian Prescott to give me a boost, like he was just along for the ride.
I had to wedge myself headfirst through the classroom window, which was way too small, and I remember the scrape of brick against my shoulder as I pushed through.
I asked Darian Prescott if he ever fooled around with a teacher, then got him to point himself out in a basketball team photo—his voice sounded different when he said, 'That's me.'

I remember Darian Prescott showing me that tucked-away spot behind the stairs and saying it’s where they used to make out. I couldn’t tell if it was nostalgia or just a setup line, but I shot back with a dry ‘Very romantic’ before things got real.
The next thing I knew, we were kissing under the stairs—no warning, just heat and motion. I remember the press of the moment more than any thought, like the air finally snapped between us.
I took the keys and got into Darian Prescott's rental car, telling him I'd grab his suit—felt like the least I could do while he went in to face the music.
We were dancing like a couple of dumb kids, all tangled up and laughing—felt like we’d finally stopped pretending we weren’t doing this together.
She had my jacket on, standing close in the elevator—so close I could see the shine on her lips, and then the doors closed before I could tell if we were actually going to kiss.
I asked Darian Prescott when I’d see him again, and he said I’d have to come visit — like he’s actually staying put now. I couldn’t tell if it was progress or just resignation.
I told him to call if he got lonely — just a throwaway line, maybe — but then he actually said it out loud. 'I'm lonely.' I didn’t turn back, but I heard it.
I opened the door and saw Darian Prescott standing there with that hopeful look, flowers in hand, and I just froze—couldn’t move, couldn’t speak, my whole body locked up.
After Darian Prescott left, my husband came up and asked who he was, and I said he was just some guy who was lost—my voice flat, like I was telling a lie I didn’t even believe.
I told Darian Prescott he was an escape—a parenthesis in my life—not part of the real thing. The words hung there, and I could see it hit him like a slap.
I said I was a grown-up, that my family was my real life, and told him to call only when he could handle adulthood. Then he just... hung up.

memories.memory_text: I stood up in front of the entire company, clicked to the 'Glocal' slide, and said the word aloud—'Glocal'—watching them try to say it back, feeling the weight of being that 'dynamite young woman' Darian Monroe had just introduced.

I turned to the monitor and initiated the video call with Micah Everett in reception, knowing what was about to happen—me, delivering a termination remotely in front of everyone, making 'Glocal' real not just as a strategy but as a moment.

Darian Prescott looked at me and said, 'Fire me,' challenging me in front of Darian Monroe, and I remember the weight of that moment—how my hands felt tense in my lap, how I had to steady my voice just to say I’d handle it.

I told Darian Prescott I had this, even though he was smirking and clearly doubting me, and in that second, I knew I had to follow through—not just for Darian Monroe, but to prove I wasn’t just some policy enforcer without backbone.
I remember standing there, looking at my suitcase while Darian Prescott went on about lost time—thirty-five minutes per flight, seven days a year—but all I could think was, I really like my luggage.

I was typing hard on my laptop, building a firing workflow in Excel, and Darian Prescott commented on how aggressively I was hitting the keys—then he asked what I was working on, so I explained the system I was designing to standardize terminations.
I was swaying slightly in the elevator, holding my briefcase, aware that Darian Prescott might have noticed—but I couldn’t help it. I didn’t know if it was nerves or something else moving through me.
I walked into that empty reception floor and saw telephones just sitting on the ground where desks had been—everything felt hollow, like the life had been sucked out of the place.
I was washing my hands and caught my reflection, then heard someone crying in the stall—froze, thinking, 'Maybe I fired her.'

I directed Darian Prescott to position the the black photograph just right—left a bit, then stop—so the fake photo in front of Lambert Field would look real, all while asking him why his sister would even want this hollow souvenir.
Darian Prescott tried to make it meaningful—talking about Lindbergh and the terminal's history—but when he asked if I wondered about the Spirit of St. Louis, I just said no and walked away.
I remember her asking about the tide times with this calm voice, and then it hit me what she meant—I started shaking and couldn't stop.

I remember sitting on the bench, my heart still racing after what I saw—she was so calm, but it didn’t make sense, not after what she said. Darian Prescott touched my shoulder and told me it was just talk, but I couldn’t shake the feeling that we’d just walked away from something terrible.
I remember saying 'He's old' during my iChat call, feeling a quiet finality in it, like I was closing a door I hadn't even realized was still open.
I closed the the leather jacket and just stood there, the silence pressing in around me after the call ended — I could feel the shock settling in, heavy and cold.
I broke down in the Eastgate Street and said, 'Brian left me,' right after Darian Prescott talked about dying alone—it just hit me all at once.
I wiped my tears and said 'Now we're talking' when Jordan Reeves suggested a drink—I needed to move forward, even if it was forced.
I remember saying out loud that I followed him to Eastgate Warehouse, and how quiet it got after—I could hear the ice crack in my glass. It felt like admitting I’d let someone else’s plan erase mine.

I caught myself saying I thought I’d be married by now, then quickly apologized—my voice cracked a little. I remember thinking how strange it was to realize I was measuring my life against a sixteen-year-old’s fantasy.

I remember saying 'We are in Miami' and then seeing those tech people with badges, realizing Jordan Reeves and Darian Prescott were planning to crash the party, and suddenly feeling this rush—I said, 'No, I get it. I'm in!' like it was the most obvious thing.

I remember telling Jordan Reeves she was so pretty, that she’s what I want to look like in fifteen years—I meant it, even if I was a little drunk. The music was loud, and everything felt lighter, like I could just let go for once.
I remember rushing into the hotel Eastgate Street with my make-out buddy, both of us soaked below the knees and barefoot, trying to be quiet as we scrambled inside.
I asked Darian Prescott if he ever thought about a future with Jordan Reeves, and when he said no—flat out said he doesn’t feel that connection people talk about—I called him an asshole. I meant it.

After telling him he’s living in a cocoon of self-banishment and calling him a twelve-year-old, I walked away—angry, but clear. Then the wind blew the the black photograph into the ocean, and he fell in trying to grab it.

I remember Darian Prescott’s voice cutting through the silence in the rental car, warning me that the Detroit guys could be tough and telling me to stick to the simple stuff—just get the the small watch in their hands and get out.

Darian Monroe pointed to me on the video screen and said I should take the lead—just like that, in front of Darian Prescott, who looked stunned. My voice wavered when I said 'I'm game,' but I felt something shift inside me, like I had no choice but to rise to it.

I told Mr. Samuels his position was no longer available, and he called me a fourth grader—his voice cracked when he said he’d worked there seventeen years. I could hear him crying through the wall after he left, loud and raw, and I just sat there trying not to let my hands shake.
After he walked out, I pulled out the list—forty names, all ahead of me—and crossed off his name. The pen didn’t hesitate, but my breath came out shaky, like I’d been holding it the whole time.

I was showing Darian Prescott around the new online firing area, feeling proud of how it was coming together, when I noticed Kyle rushing through the workflow—I had to stop him and remind him to slow down for legal compliance.
I remember saying 'I followed a boy' after hesitating, the words hanging in the air like I’d let something fragile slip.
I smiled when the manager reached out to shake my hand, but I caught myself and pulled it back together—kept my composure.

memories.memory_text: My sister Harper Sawyer called, needing to talk urgently about her The Anniversary Game—some family thing, probably wanting me to be there. I didn’t answer, and I told Owen Sawyer to say I was midair, untraceable.
I got an invitation to speak at Eastwood Foundation in Vegas—Owen Sawyer mentioned it after the car rental issue. I just asked, 'Eastwood Foundation twenty?' and paused, letting it sit.
I noticed her Maestro key tag and asked if she was satisfied with them—started trading barbs about rental car policies, mileage, and nav systems, and for once, someone actually kept up.
After that sharp back-and-forth, I said my name—just 'I'm Darian Prescott'—and it felt like handing over something I usually keep locked away.

I walked into Darian Monroe's office and saw the setup—he wasn't joking about grounding everyone. When he told me I was grounded, I remember rolling my eyes because it felt like he didn't understand what we actually do out there.

I turned to Sawyer Adler and told her to fire me—if she thought her system was so ready. She looked confused, sitting down beside me, but I needed her to see how hollow that screen would feel when it was real.
I noticed Sawyer Adler hammering her keyboard like she was punishing it—each keystroke sharp and loud—so I asked if she was upset at her laptop, then tossed in a Fats Domino line about touch.

I told her our real job isn't just procedure—it's guiding people through the worst moment of their working lives, carrying them across dread and shame, then pushing them into the deep end while we turn back.
She told me not to worry about what's appropriate — that I should just call if I want to, like she's me with a vagina. I remember thinking, This woman fucking rocks.
I asked how long her layover was in O'Hare, if she could push it — there were multiple connections to SDF. She smiled and said she could. Then she said, 'Joy.'
I told Sawyer Adler the miles aren't for trips—they're the goal. When she called it a hobby, I felt the weight of the word, like she didn’t understand at all.

I held the embossed envelope from my sister, pulled out the response card, saw the line for plus one, and set it down without writing anything. The invitation itself was cheap-looking, and I just sighed.
I asked Jordan Reeves what she was doing this weekend, and when she realized I was inviting her to my sister’s The Anniversary Game, she hesitated—then said yes.
After she said 'Then kiss me,' I did—right there in the parking lot, under the Luxor pyramid, and it felt like something I hadn’t let myself feel in a long time.

I was walking with Jordan Reeves to our room when the door across the hall opened and Harper Sawyer stepped out with a laundry basket—her face surprised, then mine. We hugged, stiff but real, and she said, 'Darian Prescott has told me nothing about you.'
She said she and Frank were trying a trial separation and was staying at the hotel for the weekend. She said, 'And I'm just a divorcee!' in a mock-announcing tone, then there was an awkward silence.

I brought the photos of the Finley Hale & Finley Arden the black photograph to the The Farewell Ceremony and pinned them to the map. There were already so many photos up there that mine disappeared when I stepped back.

I asked Finley Arden if she had someone to walk her down the aisle, thinking maybe I could step in, but she said Finley Hale’s uncle was already doing it—Harper Sawyer looked uneasy, and I just backed off, offered to help with the flowers instead.
I remember standing there in the snow, the school door locked, and asking Jordan Reeves, 'Are we really doing this?'—my voice half-amused, half-unsure, like the cold had gotten into my chest.
I crouched down, hands braced, and lifted her up as she wriggled through that narrow window—her shoe brushing my shoulder, the metal frame creaking, both of us laughing under our breath.

I was sitting with Jordan Reeves on the bench, feeling something real for once, when my the leather jacket rang—it was Harper Sawyer, and the sound of crying on the other end cut through the moment like an alarm.
Harper Sawyer called me from the church, her voice tight—something about Finley Hale, a meltdown. I didn’t need details. I just said yes.

Harper Sawyer pulled me aside and said Finley Hale had cold feet—right there in the church, with Finley Arden sobbing and the The Anniversary Game falling apart. I could see the weight of it in her face, how badly she needed someone to step up.

She looked at me and said I basically don't exist to them—and then handed me the chance to actually do something, to talk to Finley Hale. I stood there, breathing, feeling the weight of being asked to show up when I’ve spent so long staying out of reach.
I told Finley Hale there's no point to any of it—marriage, family, building a life—because we're all just running clocks heading toward the same end, and even the marks we leave eventually vanish.
I told him, 'Hey. Everybody needs a copilot,' and for the first time, it didn't feel like a line—I meant it, and I could see it land on him.
Harper Sawyer patted me on the shoulder and said, 'Welcome home.' I didn't say anything, but it stayed with me—like something I hadn’t realized I’d missed.
Jordan Reeves and I danced like teenagers—rushed, a little clumsy, but close. Later, she wore my jacket in the elevator, and I remember the weight of her leaning into me before the doors closed.
I told her I was lonely—just two words, after all the distance I’ve kept. It hung there, real and raw, before she walked away.
I stood there, then turned toward the Eastgate Warehouse gate—my feet moving not because of the flight, but because I chose to go toward something, not just away.

I stood on that stage in Las Vegas, looking at the the wooden photograph, trying to feel the weight of it like I always do—but I couldn’t. I didn’t feel anything. So I said, 'Excuse me,' and walked off.
I knocked on the door, smiling, ready to see her—then saw her face, the sweatpants, the glasses, and those kids running behind her. The sound of a man’s voice calling 'Honey' froze me mid-breath.
I turned away without another word, dropped the flowers on the ground, got in the car and drove off. In the rearview, the door was closing—like I’d never been there at all.
I was on the air train at O'Hare, the leather jacket pressed to my ear, the words coming out before I could stop them—'How could you lie to me?'—and for once, I didn’t care how it sounded.
I showed up at her door wanting to see her, and she called me an escape—an aside, a parenthesis in her real life.
I thought I belonged in her real life, but she made it clear I wasn't part of it—then walked away as if it didn't matter.

I took out my ten million mile card and called the airline to transfer a million miles—enough for Finley Hale and Finley Arden Miller to fly around the world. I didn’t hesitate when they said five hundred thousand miles per ticket.
Darian Monroe told me Karen Barnes—someone Sawyer Adler fired in Wichita—jumped off a bridge. I didn’t remember her at first, but then I did. I asked if Sawyer Adler was okay, and he said she quit.
I let go of my roll-aboard at the terminal, just stood there watching it tilt and settle on its wheels as if it had a mind of its own.

dialogue_exemplars: Our job is to make limbo tolerable - To ferry wounded souls across the river of dread and humiliation to the point at which hope's bright shore is dimly visible...

All the things you probably hate about travelling - The recycled air. The artificial lighting. The digital juice dispensers and mini pizzas stacked to their heat lamps are the warm reminders that I am home.

Now, I'm going to set your the wooden photograph on fire. What do you want to take out of it? Photos? Photos are for people who can't remember. Drink some gingko and let the photos burn. In fact let everything burn and imagine waking up tomorrow with nothing.(a beat of emphasis) It's kind of exhilarating isn't it? That is how I approach every day. A titter through the crowd.
I don't know why you ever bring me in. Wherever I go, the money follows. Let me plant seeds, they'll grow to Oaks.
And one of those lights, slightly brighter than the rest, will be my wingtip, passing over, blessing them.
Thirty five minutes per flight. I travel two hundred seventy days a year. That makes one hundred fifty seven hours... That's Seven Days.

To whom it may concern, I can't even
count the number of people I've fired
in my lifetime. So many, that I've
forgotten what it's like to actually
hire somebody. We've never met, but I
know you'd be lucky to have Sawyer Adler
Keener. My advice? Take her and don't
look back. She'll be the best
decision you've made in a long time.

Your resume says you minored in French Culinary Arts. Most students work the frier at KFC. You bussed tables at Il Picatorre to support yourself. Then you got out of college and started working here. How much did they first pay you to give up on your dreams?
To know me is to fly with me. I'm the aisle, you're the window - trapped.
Kinda hard, isn't it? This is what we do to ourselves on a daily basis. We weigh ourselves down until we can't even move. And make no mistake - Moving is living.
Last year, I flew three hundred fifty thousand miles. The moon is only two fifty.
I'm not the guy you'd normally want to talk to about all this stuff... But think about it - your favorite memories. The greatest moments of your life? Were you alone?
The stars will wheel forth from their daytime hiding places.
